lessons.title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control

before.content_html:
The Endocrine System

The endocrine system is made up of glands that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical messengers secreted directly into the blood and carried to target organs where they produce an effect. Compared to the nervous system, hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting and act on a wider area.

The pituitary gland in the brain is called the “master gland” because it produces hormones that act on other glands, stimulating them to release their own hormones. Key endocrine glands include:

  • Pituitary gland (brain) — produces growth hormone, FSH, LH, ADH, TSH.
  • Thyroid gland (neck) — produces thyroxine, which regulates metabolic rate.
  • Pancreas — produces insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose.
  • Adrenal glands (above kidneys) — produce adrenaline for the “fight or flight” response.
  • Ovaries — produce oestrogen and progesterone.
  • Testes — produce testosterone.
Key Fact

The pituitary gland is the “master gland” — it produces hormones that control other glands. Hormones travel in the blood to target organs and produce slower but longer-lasting responses than nerves.

Blood Glucose Control

Blood glucose concentration is monitored and controlled by the pancreas. When blood glucose rises (e.g. after eating), the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into cells, and stimulates the liver to convert glucose into glycogen for storage. This lowers blood glucose back to normal.

When blood glucose falls too low (e.g. during exercise or between meals), the pancreas releases glucagon. Glucagon causes the liver to convert glycogen back into glucose, which is released into the blood. This raises blood glucose back to normal. This is a classic example of negative feedback.

Key Fact

Insulin lowers blood glucose (glucose → glycogen in liver). Glucagon raises blood glucose (glycogen → glucose from liver). Both are produced by the pancreas in a negative feedback loop.

Type 1 diabetes is a condition where the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It is usually diagnosed in childhood, is not linked to lifestyle, and is treated with insulin injections. The patient must also monitor their diet and blood glucose levels.

Type 2 diabetes is where the body’s cells no longer respond to insulin properly (insulin resistance). It is linked to obesity and lifestyle factors. It is treated with a carbohydrate-controlled diet, increased exercise and sometimes medication. Type 2 diabetes is becoming more common worldwide due to rising obesity levels.

The nervous system transmits electrical impulses along neurones for fast, short-lived, localised responses. The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood for slower, longer-lasting, widespread responses. Both systems work together to coordinate body functions — for example, the hypothalamus in the brain links the two systems.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of FSH in the menstrual cycle.
practice_questions.marks: FSH is released by the pituitary gland (1). It stimulates an egg to mature in a follicle in the ovary / stimulates the ovary to produce oestrogen (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the oral contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy.
practice_questions.marks: The pill contains hormones (oestrogen and/or progesterone) (1). These inhibit the production of FSH from the pituitary gland (1). Without FSH, eggs do not mature and ovulation does not occur (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the interactions between oestrogen and the pituitary hormones during the menstrual cycle.
practice_questions.marks: Oestrogen is produced by the ovaries in response to FSH (1). At low levels, oestrogen inhibits FSH release (negative feedback) (1). At high levels, oestrogen stimulates the release of LH from the pituitary gland (positive feedback) (1). The LH surge triggers ovulation around day 14 (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of IVF as a fertility treatment.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Balanced discussion covering scientific and ethical points.
Advantages: IVF allows couples who cannot conceive naturally to have children (1). Success rates have improved with modern technology (1). Disadvantages: It is expensive and not always available on the NHS (1). It is physically and emotionally demanding for the woman (1). Multiple embryos may be implanted, increasing the risk of multiple births (1). Unused embryos may be destroyed, which raises ethical concerns for some people (1).

practice_questions.text: State one advantage of using condoms over hormonal contraceptives.
practice_questions.marks: Condoms protect against STIs / sexually transmitted infections as well as pregnancy (1).

before.content_html:
Sexual and Asexual Reproduction

There are two types of reproduction. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion (joining) of male and female gametes (sperm and egg). The offspring are genetically different from each other and from both parents, because they receive a random mix of genetic material. This genetic variation is important for natural selection.

Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes. The offspring are genetically identical to the parent — they are clones. Asexual reproduction occurs through mitosis. Many plants and some animals (e.g. bacteria, starfish) can reproduce asexually.

Key Fact

Sexual reproduction: two parents, gametes fuse, offspring are genetically varied. Asexual reproduction: one parent, mitosis only, offspring are clones. Variation in sexual reproduction is important for natural selection and survival.

Meiosis

Meiosis is the type of cell division that produces gametes (sex cells). It takes place in the reproductive organs (ovaries and testes). Before meiosis, the DNA replicates. The cell then divides twice, producing four genetically different haploid cells, each with half the chromosome number (23 in humans).

When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the full chromosome number is restored (46 in humans). The resulting cell is called a zygote, which then divides by mitosis to form an embryo.

Mitosis: one division, produces 2 identical diploid cells, used for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, produces 4 different haploid cells (gametes), used for sexual reproduction. Both start with DNA replication, but meiosis shuffles genetic material, creating variation.

DNA Structure

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made up of two strands twisted into a double helix. DNA is found in the nucleus of cells, arranged into structures called chromosomes. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total).

A gene is a short section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, which are assembled into a specific protein. The entire set of genetic material in an organism is called its genome.

Key Fact

DNA is a double helix found in chromosomes in the nucleus. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. The Human Genome Project mapped all human DNA.

The Human Genome Project was an international effort to map every gene in the human genome. Understanding the genome helps scientists identify genes linked to specific diseases, develop personalised medicines, and trace human migration patterns and evolutionary relationships.

Alleles and Inheritance

Most characteristics are controlled by several genes working together (polygenic). Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene with two forms called alleles. You inherit one allele from each parent, giving you two alleles for each gene.

If the two alleles are the same, the individual is homozygous for that gene. If they are different, the individual is heterozygous. A dominant allele is always expressed when present (shown by a capital letter, e.g. B). A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are present (bb).

Key Fact

Genotype = the combination of alleles (e.g. Bb). Phenotype = the physical characteristic expressed (e.g. brown eyes). Dominant alleles only need one copy to be expressed; recessive alleles need two copies (homozygous recessive).

Punnett Squares and Genetic Diagrams

A Punnett square is used to show the possible combinations of alleles in offspring. For example, if both parents are heterozygous (Bb):

The offspring ratios would be: \(\frac{1}{4}\) BB, \(\frac{2}{4}\) Bb, \(\frac{1}{4}\) bb. This gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive).

A couple are both carriers of cystic fibrosis (genotype Ff). What is the probability of their child having cystic fibrosis?

Parent genotypes: Ff × Ff. The Punnett square gives: FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Only ff has cystic fibrosis. So the probability is \(\frac{1}{4}\) or 25%. Note: each child has the same probability, regardless of previous children.

Inherited Disorders

Some disorders are caused by faulty alleles inherited from parents:

Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of cell membranes caused by a recessive allele (f). A person must inherit two copies (ff) to be affected. A carrier (Ff) has one copy but does not show symptoms. It causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system.

Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele. It causes extra fingers or toes. Only one copy of the dominant allele is needed to have the condition (Dd or DD).

Key Fact

Cystic fibrosis = recessive disorder (need ff to be affected; Ff = carrier). Polydactyly = dominant disorder (need only one D allele). Use Punnett squares to predict offspring ratios.

During IVF, embryos can be screened for genetic disorders before being implanted. This allows parents to select embryos that do not carry the faulty allele. However, embryo screening is controversial — some people argue it prevents suffering, while others believe it is unethical to select embryos or that it could lead to “designer babies.”

Sex Determination

In humans, sex is determined by the 23rd pair of chromosomes: XX = female, XY = male. A Punnett square shows there is a 50% chance of each sex. The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene, which triggers male development.

before.content_html:
Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering is a process where scientists modify the genetic material of an organism. A gene that codes for a useful characteristic is “cut” from one organism’s DNA and inserted into another organism’s genome. The organism that receives the new gene is called a genetically modified organism (GMO).

Key Fact

In genetic engineering, enzymes are used to isolate the required gene. This gene is then inserted into a vector (such as a bacterial plasmid or virus) which carries it into the cells of the target organism. The organism’s cells then produce the desired protein.

The process of genetic engineering follows a clear sequence of steps. First, the gene that produces the desired characteristic is identified and isolated using restriction enzymes, which cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. The gene is then inserted into a vector — typically a small ring of bacterial DNA called a plasmid. The vector carries the gene into the host organism’s cells, where it is incorporated into the DNA and expressed to produce the desired protein.

One of the most important applications is the production of human insulin by genetically modified bacteria. The human insulin gene is inserted into bacterial plasmids, and the bacteria then produce insulin in large quantities. This replaced the older method of extracting insulin from pig or cow pancreases, which sometimes caused allergic reactions in patients.

GM crops have been engineered to be resistant to insect attack or to produce higher yields. For example, Bt corn contains a gene from a soil bacterium that produces a natural insecticide, reducing the need for chemical pesticides. Golden rice has been modified to produce beta-carotene (a source of vitamin A) to help combat vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

Benefits and Risks of Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering has significant potential benefits. In agriculture, GM crops can increase food production by improving resistance to pests, disease and herbicides. This can help feed a growing world population. In medicine, genetic engineering allows large-scale production of useful proteins such as insulin and growth hormone.

However, there are concerns. Some people worry that GM crops could have unknown effects on human health if consumed over long periods. There are also ecological concerns — genes from GM plants could spread to wild populations through cross-pollination, potentially creating “superweeds” that are resistant to herbicides. Ethical concerns exist about whether it is right to modify the genes of living organisms, particularly when it comes to genetic modification of animals or potential future modifications of human embryos.

Key Fact

You are expected to evaluate the benefits and risks of genetic engineering. Benefits include: disease-resistant crops, higher yields, medical protein production. Risks include: unknown long-term health effects, gene transfer to wild populations, and ethical concerns.

Ecosystems and Communities

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. Ecosystems can range in size from a small pond to an entire ocean. Within an ecosystem, organisms are organised into levels.

A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting together in an area. A population is all the organisms of one species in a given area. A habitat is the place where an organism lives. Each species has its own role within the community, known as its niche.

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that influence where organisms can live. These include light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH and mineral content, wind speed and direction, and carbon dioxide levels (for plants) or oxygen levels (for aquatic organisms).

Biotic factors are living factors that affect organisms in an ecosystem. These include availability of food, the introduction of new predators or competitors, and the arrival of new pathogens (disease-causing organisms). Changes in any biotic or abiotic factor can affect the distribution and population size of species in a community.

Competition and Interdependence

Organisms within a community compete for resources. Animals compete for food, territory, mates and water. Plants compete for light, water, space and mineral ions from the soil. If two species are competing for the same niche, one will usually out-compete the other. Within a community, species depend on each other for food, shelter, seed dispersal and pollination — this is called interdependence. If one species is removed, the whole community can be affected.

A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain roughly the same. Examples include tropical rainforests and ancient oak woodlands. In these ecosystems, the populations of predators and prey, producers and consumers are balanced over time.

Feeding Relationships and Trophic Levels

Trophic levels describe the position of an organism in a food chain. Producers (usually green plants or algae) are at trophic level 1 — they photosynthesise to make their own food. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat the producers and are at trophic level 2. Secondary consumers (carnivores) eat the primary consumers and are at trophic level 3. Tertiary consumers are at trophic level 4.

Key Fact

Producers are the starting point of all food chains because they transfer energy from the Sun into biomass through photosynthesis. All consumers depend — directly or indirectly — on producers for their energy.

Predators kill and eat other animals (their prey). In a stable community, the populations of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles. When the prey population increases, more food is available for predators, so the predator population also increases. This then causes the prey population to fall (more are eaten), which in turn causes the predator population to decline. This repeating pattern is known as the predator-prey cycle.

Decomposers (mainly bacteria and fungi) break down dead plant and animal matter through the process of decay. This returns mineral ions and nutrients to the soil, where they can be taken up again by plants. Decomposition is faster in warm, moist, aerobic conditions. Decomposers are essential for nutrient cycling in ecosystems.

Energy is transferred along food chains, but not all energy passes from one trophic level to the next. At each level, energy is lost to the surroundings through life processes — organisms use energy for movement, keeping warm, and other metabolic reactions. Energy is also lost in waste products (faeces and urine) and through respiration. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels — there is not enough energy left to support organisms beyond that point.

knowledge_checks.q: In genetic engineering, what is the role of a vector such as a bacterial plasmid?
options: It identifies and isolates the required gene from the donor organism
It removes unwanted genes from the host organism's DNA
It carries the isolated gene into the cells of the target organism
It produces the desired protein directly without entering any cell

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an ecological risk associated with GM crops?
options: Genes spreading to wild plant populations through cross-pollination, potentially creating herbicide-resistant weeds
GM crops producing less food than conventional varieties
Bacteria used in production becoming unable to reproduce
The cost of restriction enzymes making GM crops unaffordable

In a stable community, the populations of predators and prey fluctuate in a repeating pattern called the _____.
Match each ecology term to its correct definition.
right: All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area at the same time
The role of a species within an ecosystem, including what it eats, what eats it, and how it interacts
Organisms such as bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter, returning nutrients to the soil
